title: Metrics Monitoring
seoTitle: Design a Metrics Monitoring System Like Datadog
description: Design a metrics monitoring and alerting system — collecting time-series metrics from thousands of hosts, storing them efficiently, querying dashboards and firing alerts.
author: Editorial Team

blocks.title: What is a Metrics Monitoring System?
blocks.text: A metrics monitoring system (like Datadog or Prometheus) collects numeric measurements — CPU usage, request latency, error counts — from servers and applications, shows them on dashboards, and alerts engineers when something looks wrong.

items: Services should be able to emit metrics (name, tags, value, timestamp).
Users should be able to query metrics over time ranges for dashboards, with aggregation (avg, max, p99) and grouping by tags.
Users should be able to define alert rules (e.g. "error rate > 5% for 5 minutes") and be notified when they fire.

blocks.question: What are the non-functional requirements for this system?

items: Ingest ~10M data points per second from ~100k hosts.
Dashboards over the last few hours should load in < 1s.
Alerts should fire within ~1 minute of a condition becoming true.
Ingestion should be highly available; losing a tiny fraction of points during failures is acceptable, but the pipeline must not fall over.
Retain data for a year, at lower resolution for older data.

blocks.text: This is a **write-heavy time-series** problem. The decisions that matter are how we absorb the ingest rate, how we store points compactly so queries are fast, and how we evaluate alerts continuously without hammering storage.

items: **Metric series**: a metric name plus a unique set of tags (e.g. `http.latency{service=api, region=us-east}`).
**Alert rule**: a query, a threshold, a duration, and notification targets.
**Alert**: an instance of a rule firing or resolving.

blocks.text: 1) Services should be able to emit metrics

An **agent** on each host collects local metrics and application metrics, aggregates them over 10 seconds, and sends batches to an **Ingestion Service**. Batching on the host turns millions of tiny writes into far fewer requests.
2) Users should be able to query metrics for dashboards

A **Query Service** parses queries, fetches the relevant series for the time range from the time-series database, and aggregates them — grouping by tags and rolling up into steps (e.g. one point per minute).
3) Users should be able to define alerts

Alert rules are stored in a relational database. An **Alert Evaluator** runs each rule's query on a schedule (e.g. every 30 seconds), tracks how long the condition has held, and sends notifications through a notification service when a rule fires or resolves.
1) How do we absorb 10M points per second reliably?

blocks.title: Write directly from the API into the database

approach.text: The Ingestion Service writes each batch synchronously to storage.

challenges.text: Any storage slowdown backs up ingestion and agents start dropping data. Spikes (a deploy restarting every host) can overwhelm the database.

approach.text: The Ingestion Service validates batches and appends them to **Kafka**, partitioned by series ID so each series is written in order by one consumer. Storage writers consume at their own pace; if storage is slow, Kafka absorbs the backlog for hours. Agents also buffer locally and retry if ingestion is briefly unavailable.

challenges.text: Data appears on dashboards slightly behind real time (seconds), which is fine. Partition count must be planned for growth.

blocks.text: 2) How do we store time-series data efficiently?

blocks.title: A row per data point in a relational database

challenges.text: Billions of rows per day, massive indexes, and slow range scans — row-oriented storage wastes space on repetitive data.

blocks.title: A purpose-built time-series store with compression and downsampling

approach.text: Group points into blocks per series per time window (e.g. 2 hours). Compress timestamps with **delta-of-delta** encoding and values with **XOR (Gorilla) encoding** — regular metrics compress to about 1-2 bytes per point. Keep raw 10s data for ~2 weeks, then **downsample** to 1-minute and 1-hour rollups (min, max, sum, count) for long-term retention. Use an inverted index from tags to series IDs so `{service=api}` finds matching series instantly.

challenges.text: High-cardinality tags (like `userId`) explode the number of series and the index. Enforce cardinality limits per metric.

blocks.text: Cardinality is the number one way monitoring systems fall over in practice. A single metric tagged with a request ID can create millions of series overnight.
3) How do we evaluate alerts quickly without hammering storage?

blocks.title: Evaluate rules by querying the TSDB on a schedule

approach.text: Every 30 seconds, run each rule's query against recent data.

challenges.text: Tens of thousands of rules × frequent queries is a heavy, constant load on the database that dashboards also depend on.

approach.text: Alert evaluators consume the same Kafka stream and maintain in-memory rolling windows for only the series referenced by alert rules. Conditions are evaluated as points arrive; state ("condition true since 12:03") is checkpointed so evaluators can restart without losing track. Rules are sharded across evaluators.

challenges.text: More complex than polling, and complex queries spanning long windows may still need the TSDB. A hybrid of both is common.

quiz.question: Why put Kafka between ingestion and storage?
options: It absorbs spikes and storage slowdowns so ingestion never backs up
quiz.explanation: The log buffers data durably while storage writers catch up.

quiz.question: What is downsampling?
options: Replacing old high-resolution points with coarser rollups like 1-minute min/max/avg
quiz.explanation: Rollups keep long-term trends at a fraction of the storage.

quiz.question: Why are high-cardinality tags dangerous?
options: Each unique tag combination creates a new series, exploding storage and index size
quiz.explanation: Tags like userId or requestId can create millions of series.

quiz.question: Which encoding makes timestamps at regular intervals extremely compact?
quiz.explanation: Regular intervals produce deltas-of-deltas of zero, which need almost no bits.
